title: 1917 Chicago show band photograph and the lost drum deposit
summary: Keppard describes the band photographed in Chicago in 1917 as manager, the lost drum deposit, and cornetist Sugar Johnny and his furniture swindles.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: If you could tell us about some of the men on this picture.

You see now this here, this picture here, her husband is on this photograph, is her husband is the manager of the shore. Now she is black enough to impotate. She was a white person. She's a white person but she's black enough. This is nothing but a drop scenery but it's in Chicago, Illinois. That's during 1917. Now she's black enough to entertain. She's the dancer. Now her husband is the manager of the show. He's what they call a booking agent. That's her husband. And now the violin, he's leading the band. That's Johnny Lindsey. That's me on the guitar, Lloyd Kephart. There's Johnny, I mean there's Eric Garland on bass. Now all them is from New Orleans. He's straight from New Orleans. Well the manager, I ain't talking about the booking agent, I'm talking about Mr. Photo said they don't need no drum. They don't need no drum because they got a drum over there already. So we never brought the drum but of course, nevertheless, we had suggested to bring Lil Happy, which used to play at the Little Theatre with Roby's Show. I ain't talking about Happy, I'm talking about Little Red Happy. We had suggested to give him, to get him to come with us. But we got a telegram not to bring no drum. And they had give us, they had give me as the manager of the band, they gave me the money to make a deposit of $25 each man. And they would send the tickets and the transportation to go and come with us. But that $25 is only a deposit for the man's if they need anything provided they want to buy something. So I turned around and I gave, Eddie, or gives Red Happy the $25 expecting that he was going to be with us. You understand? Yeah. But after I gave him the $25, I got a telegram down here suggesting and saying that they don't bring no drum because they got a drum up there already. Well, I said, well that's money, what I give is dead money. That's true, you know? Yeah. Because I hadn't stopped the man and that was his $25 deposit. Well if anybody's losing, well it'll be the company because I was authorized to give this money deposit to each and every man to hold him, you know? Well, and then he signed his name to it. Well after he signed his name to it, that money's dead. So anyhow, well I went to Happy and I told Happy about it. I said, Happy, I'm very sorry that I can't bring you with us, but Mr. Lacazza say that the money that you got on the deposit, you keep it. He said, because that was your forfeit. He said, no. He says, I read it ago. He told me. He read Happy. Poor fellow is dead. I'm sorry. He wasn't easily listening. But he's listening anyhow in his grave. So to help with the Lord, he is listening. Because they say spirits walk. They hear everything. They can see you, hear you, but you can't see them, you can't hear them, you know? They're spirits. They're all around the world talking. Of course I don't know. I never see nobody dead, nobody die yet and come back and tell me how it was. But nonetheless, he got that $25 and he kept it. I said, well, all right, but he didn't want that money. He wanted to go along. Well, I tell him it's no use. I can't because they just sent enough tickets, this for us. You know, for us five men sent enough, send six. But that $25, what you have, you just keep it. Well, of course I understand he hadn't spent it before that telegram. Gosh, I don't know that. Of course that was spent money. Well anyhow, then Lawrence Dewey, he got up there. Sugar County, of course they call him Johnny Smith.
To get back to Dewey, was he working here in town? Was he working here?
